data.title: Citizenship status as a hiring ground is unlawful unless a rule requires it (8 U.S.C. § 1324b)
data.summary: US law makes it "an unfair immigration-related employment practice for a person or other entity to discriminate against any individual … with respect to the hiring, or recruitment or referral for a fee, of the individual for employment" because of national origin or, for a protected individual, citizenship status. The exception at § 1324b(a)(2) is the operative part here: citizenship-based discrimination is permitted only where it is "required in order to comply with law, regulation, or executive order, or required by Federal, State, or local government contract". So a rejection that names the right to be employed somewhere is either a requirement someone can point to, or it is unlawful — and the statute obliges the employer to be able to tell the two apart. It reaches recruitment and referral, not only the hiring decision itself. It says nothing about where a candidate lives or which hours they can cover: those are not protected grounds, and a rejection naming them is outside this statute entirely. It binds US employers of more than three people, and it establishes what is permitted, never that any particular rejection occurred.
